questions.q: What does placing a checkpointLocation inside a Unity Catalog volume add over an ungoverned path?
options: READ VOLUME grants now control who can inspect the stream's offset state
It removes the need for a checkpoint location entirely
It automatically converts the stream to batch processing
It makes the streaming query run measurably faster
questions.explain: A checkpoint inside a volume inherits Unity Catalog governance, so access to the offset state itself becomes a granted permission.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what kind of files does a volume govern beyond CSV landing-zone data?
options: Only files that will eventually become a Delta table
Nothing — volumes exclusively hold structured tabular data
Any non-tabular file — trained models, PDFs, images — with the same GRANT/REVOKE mechanism as tables
Only files smaller than 1 MB
questions.explain: Volumes govern any file type, including ones that were never going to be a table at all, like model artifacts or PDFs.

questions.q: What did Databricks & Delta Lake Lesson 45 already cover in full?
options: Auto Loader's file notification mode
Storing Structured Streaming checkpoints inside a volume
What a volume is, its path shape, and creating managed/external volumes
Governing non-tabular files like PDFs and model artifacts
questions.explain: This lesson explicitly recaps Lesson 45's definition before covering the file-access patterns that lesson's single example didn't show.

questions.q: Before volumes existed, how were files like model artifacts or product images typically governed?
options: Effectively without governance, via DBFS root or an unmanaged mount
They could not be stored in Databricks at all
Through a separate Kubernetes-based access system
With the exact same row-level security as Delta tables
questions.explain: Before Unity Catalog volumes, non-tabular files typically lived in ungoverned storage like DBFS root.

questions.q: Why does this lesson describe a volume as more than 'just a folder'?
options: Because volumes are only usable from the command line, never from Spark
Because it's the general governance answer for any file, tabular or not, including files a pipeline uses internally that no user ever queries
Because a folder and a volume are technically identical concepts with no real difference
Because a volume can never actually store more than one file
questions.explain: A volume's real value is governing any file — checkpoints included — not just serving as a CSV landing zone.
